literature.cite: Simmons, K. M., and D. Sutter, 2008: Tornado Warnings, Lead Times, and Tornado Casualties: An Empirical Investigation. Weather and Forecasting, 23, 246-258. doi:10.1175/2007WAF2006027.1
literature.read: passages through a full-text extraction of the publisher's article page (journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/wefo/23/2/2007waf2006027_1.xml); a direct request answered 403. Not the whole article.
passages: a warning in effect reduces expected injuries by 32%, and an extra minute of lead time on a warning reduces expected injuries by 1.1%.
A warning in effect has almost no effect on expected fatalities—a statistically insignificant 1% decrease—while a 1-min increase in lead time increases expected fatalities by 0.6%.
The signs of the LEAD16–20, LEAD21–30, and LEAD31+ interval variables are all positive, with point estimates of 60%, 37%, and 1% increases in expected fatalities, respectively, relative to no warning
For fatalities, an increase in population density significantly increases expected fatalities, both directly and through the LENGTH × DENSITY interaction term.
